clue.text: Not surf-riding, even in the frozen North

definitions.text: Not surf-riding, even in the frozen North

parts.words: Not surf-riding, even in the frozen North
parts.note: a roller is a big breaking wave, so riding rollers sounds like surfing; the sport meant is gliding on wheels, a summer stand-in for what people do on ice up north

explanation.surface: Someone in the icy far north is plainly not out on a surfboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roller' is a long sea wave, which is why 'surf-riding' comes up; the rollers here are wheels, and the second half of the answer is what the frozen North does on its ice.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastime on wheeled boots that copies ice skating on hard ground, no waves involved.

clue.text: Haberdashery emporium ? It's poor planning

definitions.meaning: a shop selling trimmings could be called a building for ribbons
a ribbon of houses strung along a main road out of town, a sprawl planners deplore

explanation.surface: A critic attacks the design of a big drapery store.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally, a store for ribbons; as a planning term, houses built in a long line beside a road, widely criticised as sprawl.

clue.text: A jester turns up in Bath

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up reads the words a and jester from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a jester is a fool

explanation.surface: A court clown arrives in the city of Bath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turns up' reverses the whole of A FOOL. Bath, a capital here only because it opens the phrase, is the tub, not the Somerset city.
explanation.definitionFit: A dried fibrous gourd used as a bath sponge for scrubbing the skin.

clue.text: The anagram I got is in a clue that's turned up, praise be

indicators.note: the phrase is in tells us the jumble sits inside the next piece
in a down clue, turned up means the word clue is written bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the clue states outright that the words which follow are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A setter admires their own anagram, cheering a clue that has appeared.
explanation.walkthrough: Three signals work together: 'The anagram' scrambles the words after it, 'that's turned up' reads the clue word upwards as in a down light, and 'is in' sets the jumble inside it. 'Praise be' stands loosely for an adjective of praising.
explanation.definitionFit: Full of praise and commendation, as a speech honouring someone is.

clue.text: Sees about a bad dog — ties up

indicators.note: about means one word wraps around the other here, with sees placed round the dog

parts.note: a cur is a mongrel or ill-tempered dog

explanation.surface: Someone notices a vicious mongrel and tethers it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sees' is taken as written and opened up to hold CUR.
explanation.definitionFit: To fasten something firmly, binding it so it cannot move.

clue.text: Milton wrote when it was intended to the city

definitions.text: Milton wrote when it was intended to the city

parts.words: Milton wrote when it was intended to the city
parts.note: Milton's sonnet is titled 'When the ... was intended to the City', written as royalist troops threatened London in 1642; the missing word of the title is wanted

explanation.surface: A note on what a poet wrote when a plan for London was in the air.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes Milton's Sonnet VIII, 'When the Assault was Intended to the City'; 'it' stands for the missing word of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent attack on a place, the royalist attack London feared in 1642.

clue.text: Measure of Scots insularity

definitions.meaning: a small imperial unit of length, a twelfth of a foot
in Scotland and Ireland the word is used for a small island

explanation.surface: A gauge of how isolated the Scots are.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of length equal to 2.54 centimetres; in Scottish place names it means an island.

clue.text: Sound range of P.O. banking good for the balance

indicators.note: sound tells us to take a word as it is spoken and enter a different spelling

parts.note: the Giro was the Post Office's banking service
range means scope, as in the scope of a study

explanation.surface: A sound selection of Post Office banking makes for a healthy balance.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Giro was the British Post Office's money-transfer bank; said out loud it is the same as GYRO. 'Balance' is stability, not a bank account.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinning wheel in a mounting that resists tilting, used to keep ships and aircraft stable.

clue.text: Tennyson's grievous inertia

parts.note: Tennyson's lyric from The Princess is named for weeping that has no purpose; grievous gives the weeping, inertia the idleness

explanation.surface: A critic sums up the poet's sorrowful listlessness.
explanation.walkthrough: The title of Tennyson's song from The Princess is a word for crying, a word for doing nothing, and the crying again.
explanation.definitionFit: A Tennyson poem about weeping with no cause, matching grief that does nothing.

clue.text: Without these one might feel footloose

definitions.text: Without these one might feel footloose

parts.words: Without these one might feel footloose
parts.note: footloose normally means free to roam, but here it means a foot sitting loose in its shoe because nothing ties it

explanation.surface: A free spirit explains what is missing from a life with no ties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Footloose' is read literally: the shoe is loose on the foot when the strings that fasten it are absent.
explanation.definitionFit: Cords threaded through eyelets to tie a shoe or boot firmly on the foot.

clue.text: Do so, Doone

parts.note: The clue tells him to do what his first name says

explanation.surface: An order given to a member of the Doone clan.
explanation.walkthrough: In R. D. Blackmore's novel Lorna Doone, the outlaw is called Carver Doone; telling 'Doone' to 'do so' asks him to live up to that name, i.e. to do the slicing a carver does.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut meat into slices at table, the job of a carver.

clue.text: Ring and ring in the past, primate

parts.note: a ring is round, like the letter O
the past tense of ring is rang

explanation.surface: A bell that kept ringing long ago gets mixed up with an ape.
explanation.walkthrough: The two rings do different jobs: the first is a shape, giving O; the second is the verb, put in the past tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for orang-utan, the red-haired great ape of Borneo and Sumatra.

clue.text: Defeat of the old party

definitions.meaning: a heavy, disorderly defeat in battle or sport
an archaic word for a large fashionable evening gathering

explanation.surface: A political party of yesteryear suffers a drubbing.
explanation.definitionFit: A crushing defeat is a rout, and in older English a rout was a crowded society reception.

clue.text: One shilling (Edwardian?) in foreign currency

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
s was the abbreviation for the old British shilling
ER, Edwardus Rex, is the royal cipher of King Edward

explanation.surface: Someone converts a single old shilling from Edward's reign abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Currency' means a flow or current, so 'foreign currency' is a river abroad; the Iser runs through Bohemia. The shilling was a pre-1971 British coin worth twelve pence.
explanation.definitionFit: A current is something that flows, and the Iser is a flowing river in central Europe.

clue.text: Queenly bric-a brac

parts.note: knick-knacks named after a queen, namely the period of Britain's longest-reigning nineteenth-century monarch

explanation.surface: Ornaments fit for a queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornaments and collectables from the reign of Queen Victoria, 1837 to 1901.

clue.text: Surfaces suited to rubbers

parts.note: rubbers here are people making rubbings of engraved church memorial plates, not erasers or bridge games

explanation.surface: Advice on which surfaces suit erasers, or card players.
explanation.walkthrough: Brass rubbing is the British hobby of laying paper over an engraved brass plate in a church floor and rubbing it with wax to copy the figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Engraved metal memorial plates set in church floors, a favourite subject for rubbing.

clue.text: Isle o' Man a medley of irregularities

indicators.note: a medley is a mixture, so the letters of the words that follow are mixed up

explanation.surface: The Isle of Man is a jumble of oddities.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder comes before the indicator: ISLE O MAN A, nine letters, is mixed by 'a medley of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that depart from the normal rule are deviations or oddities.

clue.text: Destination of a round tour at £1

parts.note: a tour is a trip
something round is shaped like the letter O
L, from Latin libra, is the abbreviation behind the pound sign
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A package holiday going round somewhere for a single pound.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR read '£1' as '!'; the page prints 'at £1'. The pieces come in answer order: the tour first, then the round shape, then the pound and the one.
explanation.definitionFit: Libya's capital is a city travellers head for, so it can stand as a place to go.

clue.text: Opportunity for a dashing display, my darling

definitions.text: Opportunity for a dashing display, my darling

parts.words: Opportunity for a dashing display, my darling
parts.note: dashing means sweeping quickly back and forth, as an iron does over a shirt, not looking smart; the endearment makes it a household chore offered to a spouse

explanation.surface: A lover offers a partner the chance to cut a fine figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dashing' suggests stylish good looks, but the display is the iron dashing to and fro over the laundry.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressing clothes smooth with a hot flat iron, done in quick sweeping strokes.

clue.text: Caper causes American state doctor trouble

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for Georgia
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification
ado is fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: A prank lands a medic in hot water in the States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caper' looks like a scheme; it is a leap.
explanation.definitionFit: A gambado is a leap or frisky bound, as a capering horse makes.

clue.text: Over normal temperature, yet in good health, this spring

parts.note: above normal temperature means hot
in good health means well

explanation.surface: Someone runs a temperature yet feels fine, thanks to a local spa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' is a water source, not a season: a hot well is a spring of naturally warm water.
explanation.definitionFit: A natural source of warm water rising from the ground.

clue.text: Londoners will find three directions in the hall

indicators.note: in places the compass points inside the word hall

parts.note: taken as written, the word hall itself
N, W and E are compass points: north, west and east

explanation.surface: Lost Londoners are told to follow the signs in the hall.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: Hanwell is a district of west London, a place Londoners will find on their doorstep.
explanation.definitionFit: A suburb in the borough of Ealing, so a place inside the capital that its residents can reach.

clue.text: Transvestite tedium

definitions.meaning: as an adjective, in ... means dressed in clothes of the opposite sex

explanation.surface: A cross-dresser finds life dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross-dressing is called going in drag, and a dull chore is a drag.

clue.text: Where 21 goes for a guide

indicators.note: when the word from 21 goes, it leaves the rest of the longer word behind

parts.note: a dragoman is an interpreter and guide in Arabic- or Turkish-speaking lands
21 across is drag

explanation.surface: Someone asks where the answer to 21 should travel to find a guide.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference makes this look like directions; in fact DRAGOMAN (a Middle Eastern interpreter-guide) loses DRAG, and 'Where' is the definition, a place.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arabian sultanate is a place, so it answers the question of location.

clue.text: I fret to make good

indicators.note: in this old-style clue the little word to is all that signals the letters of the phrase being turned into another word

explanation.surface: A worrier frets in order to put things right.
explanation.walkthrough: The only signal for rearranging I FRET is 'to'; older Times clues often gave anagrams almost bare like this.
explanation.definitionFit: To refit a ship or building is to repair and re-equip it, restoring it to working order.

clue.text: Sweet " stuff "

definitions.meaning: a soft confection made of sugar, butter and milk
stuff, as an exclamation, means nonsense, the same as the old cry of disbelief

explanation.surface: A box of confectionery described in quotation marks.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks show that 'stuff' is the dismissive exclamation, as in 'stuff and nonsense'.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft milky confection; also an old exclamation meaning rubbish or nonsense.

clue.text: She'd look villainous wearing a mac

definitions.text: She'd look villainous wearing a mac

parts.words: She'd look villainous wearing a mac
parts.note: a mac is a raincoat on the surface, but here the letters mac go in front of a woman's name to make a Shakespearean villain

explanation.surface: A woman would seem sinister in a raincoat.
explanation.walkthrough: A mac is a British raincoat; 'wearing a mac' instead puts MAC before the name, giving Macbeth, Shakespeare's murderous king.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name, short for Elizabeth, which becomes a villain's name with Mac in front.

clue.text: Sound the north river

parts.note: the Oise is a river in northern France

explanation.surface: A command to sound the alarm on a northern river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like a verb or a water inlet; it is a noun, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sound is something heard, and so is a din.

clue.text: Rose Queen

definitions.meaning: the Danish-born consort of Edward VII

explanation.surface: A rose queen crowned at a village fete.
explanation.definitionFit: There is a rose cultivar of that name, and Queen Alexandra was wife of King Edward VII.

clue.text: Now life takes on a certain formlessness for them

definitions.text: Now life takes on a certain formlessness for them

parts.words: Now life takes on a certain formlessness for them
parts.note: a form is a school class in Britain, so formlessness is being out of any class, not shapelessness

explanation.surface: A philosophical note about people whose lives have lost shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form' is the British word for a school year group; those who have just finished school belong to no form any more.
explanation.definitionFit: Pupils who have just finished their schooling and gone out into the world.
